questions.question: Which among the following is an electron deficient compound?
questions.explanation: BH₃ (borane) is electron‐deficient because boron has only three valence electrons. Each B–H bond provides two electrons, so boron ends up with just six electrons (an incomplete octet). In contrast, NH₃, PH₃, and AsH₃ all achieve octets on their central atoms (nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic) and are not electron‐deficient.

questions.question: The octet rule is observed in
questions.explanation: In CO₂, carbon forms two double bonds with oxygen atoms, giving each atom exactly eight electrons in its valence shell, thereby obeying the octet rule. In contrast, PCl₅ and SF₆ both exhibit expanded octets (10 and 12 electrons around the central atom), while BCl₃ has only six electrons on boron (incomplete octet).

questions.question: Which of the following is correct for the process of formation of a chemical bond?
options: Electron-electron repulsion becomes more than the nucleus-electron attraction.
Energy of the system does not change.
questions.explanation: When a chemical bond forms, the attractive forces (nucleus–electron) outweigh the repulsive forces, lowering the overall potential energy of the system. This energy decrease is released, often as heat. Thus, bond formation is favored when it leads to a more stable (lower‐energy) arrangement of electrons and nuclei.

questions.question: An odd electron molecule among the following is
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) has a total of 15 electrons (7 from N and 8 from O), making it an odd‐electron molecule (a radical). By contrast, CO, SO₂, and CO₂ all have an even number of electrons and do not qualify as odd‐electron (radical) species.

questions.question: The formal charge on carbon atom in carbonate ion is:
questions.explanation: In the usual resonance form of CO₃²⁻, carbon is double‐bonded to one O (neutral) and single‐bonded to two O⁻. Formal charge on carbon is computed as: FC(C) = (Valence e⁻ of C) – [Nonbonding e⁻ + ½(Bonding e⁻)] = 4 – [0 + ½(8)] = 0 Therefore, the formal charge on the carbon atom is zero.

questions.question: Expanded octet is present in
questions.explanation: SF₆ (12 electrons around sulfur), PCl₅ (10 electrons around phosphorus), and IF₇ (14 electrons around iodine) all exceed the octet. Because they involve third‐ (or higher‐) period central atoms capable of using d orbitals, each forms an expanded octet structure.

questions.question: Molecule which follows octet rule
questions.explanation: CCl₄ has carbon with four single bonds to chlorine, giving an octet (eight electrons) around carbon. Each chlorine also completes its octet via the shared and lone pairs. By contrast, ClO₂, NO, and NO₂ all contain an odd number of electrons or otherwise violate the simple octet rule.

questions.question: In which of the following molecule, central atom has less than 8 electrons in outermost orbit?
questions.explanation: Boron in BF₃ has only three valence electrons and forms three B–F bonds, resulting in just six electrons around boron—an incomplete octet. In SnCl₄, tin achieves an octet by forming four bonds, while PCl₅ has an expanded octet (10 electrons around phosphorus), not fewer than eight. Hence, only BF₃ has a central atom with fewer than eight electrons.

questions.question: The formal charges on the three {O} -atoms in {O}_{3} molecule are:
questions.explanation: In the O₃ molecule, the formal charges on the oxygen atoms are 0, +1, and -1. The central oxygen has a formal charge of +1, while the two terminal oxygen atoms carry formal charges of 0 and -1. This results from resonance structures where the charge is delocalized.

questions.question: If stability were attained with 6 electrons rather than with 8 electrons, what would be the formula of the stable fluoride ion
questions.explanation: Neutral fluorine has 7 valence electrons. If the stable configuration required 6 valence electrons, fluorine would lose one electron rather than gain one. The stable ion would therefore be F⁺

questions.question: Which of the following shows the Lewis dot formula for {CO}_{2} ?
questions.explanation: CO₂ (carbon dioxide) has a linear structure: O=C=O. Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete its octet. Each oxygen has 6 valence electrons and needs 2 more. In the Lewis structure: Carbon forms double bonds with each oxygen atom. Each oxygen has two lone pairs (4 dots), and carbon has no lone pairs. Thus, the correct Lewis structure is: :Ö::C::Ö:

questions.question: Which of the following molecules does not have coordinate bonds?
questions.explanation: PH₄⁺ is formed by PH₃ donating a lone pair to H⁺ (a coordinate bond). NO₂ can be described (via resonance) with one O donating a pair to N. O₃ has a resonance form where the negative end donates a pair to the positive center, viewed as a dative bond. CO32- is best represented by conventional single/double bonds in resonance, with no genuine coordinate bond.

questions.question: Which of the following molecules has no dative bond?
questions.explanation: CO is commonly described (in one resonance form) with a dative bond from carbon to oxygen. SO₄²⁻ can be drawn (in certain canonical forms) with dative bonds from oxide ions to sulfur. CO₃²⁻ (carbonate) is best represented by resonance among three equivalent C–O bonds, all treated as conventional (two‐electron) covalent bonds. Thus, it does not have a true coordinate (dative) bond.

questions.question: The ion that is isoelectronic with CO is
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) has a total of 14 electrons (C = 6, O = 8). The cyanide ion (CN⁻) also has 14 electrons (C = 6, N = 7, plus one extra for the negative charge). Hence, CN⁻ is isoelectronic with CO.

questions.question: Which of the following molecules has more than one lone pair?
questions.explanation: In SO₂, sulfur has just one lone pair (with two S=O double bonds). In XeF₂, xenon has three lone pairs (and two Xe–F bonds), so well over one lone pair. SiF₄ and CH₄ each have zero lone pairs on the central atom. Hence, only XeF₂ has more than one lone pair.

questions.question: The pair of compounds having identical shapes for their molecules is
questions.explanation: XeF₂ is a linear molecule (central Xe with three lone pairs plus two bonding pairs). ZnCl₂, considered in the molecular (vapour) phase, is also linear around the Zn atom. Hence, XeF2{XeF_2} and ZnCl2{ZnCl_2} share the same molecular shape (linear). The other pairs listed have different geometries.

questions.question: Number of b . p . and l . p . on {N} atom in {NO}_{3}^{-} is
questions.explanation: In a typical (resonance) description of NO₃⁻, nitrogen is double‐bonded to one oxygen and single‐bonded to the other two. A double bond counts as two electron pairs (one σ + one π), and each single bond has one pair. Hence the N atom is involved in 4 shared‐pair (bond‐pair) electrons total and has no lone pair.

questions.question: Which of the following is not tetrahedral?
questions.explanation: CCl₄, SiF₄, and ClO₄⁻ (perchlorate) are all tetrahedral around their central atom. SF₆, however, has six ligands arranged octahedrally. Therefore, SF₆ is not tetrahedral.

questions.question: Among the following molecules: {SO}_{2}, {SF}_{4}, {CIF}_{3} , {BrF}_{5} and {XeF}_{4} which of the following shapes does not describe any of the molecules mentioned?
questions.explanation: SO₂ is bent (V‐shaped). SF₄ is see‐saw. ClF₃ is T‐shaped. BrF₅ is square pyramidal. XeF₄ is square planar. None of these molecules are perfectly trigonal bipyramidal, so (2) “Trigonal bipyramidal” does not describe any of them.

questions.question: The shape of XeOF2 on the basis of VSEPR theory is
questions.explanation: XeOF₂ has three “regions” of bonding (the O double bond counts as one region, plus two Xe–F single bonds) and two lone pairs on Xe. That makes five electron pairs in total (3 bp + 2 lp), corresponding to a trigonal‐bipyramidal arrangement. Placing the two lone pairs equatorially forces the three bonds into a “T‐shaped” geometry.

questions.question: Out of {N}_{2} {O}, {SO}_{2}, {I}_{3}^{+}, {I}_{3}^{-}, {H}_{2} {O}, {NO}_{2}^{-} and {N}_{3}^{-} , the linear species are:
questions.explanation: N₂O is a linear oxide of nitrogen. I₃⁻ (triiodide ion) is well‐known to be linear. N₃⁻ (azide ion) is also linear. By contrast, SO₂ and NO₂ are bent, H₂O is bent, and neutral “I₃” isn’t typically a discrete linear molecule. Thus, the linear species listed are N₂O, I₃⁻, and N₃⁻.
